title: What Google Cloud announced in AI this month
summary:
Editor’s note: Want to keep up with the latest from Google Cloud? Check back here for a monthly recap of our latest updates, announcements, resources, events, learning opportunities, and more.

This October, we took massive leaps forward in delivering flexible, open, and powerful enterprise AI solutions. From bringing Gemini 4 Argon to Google Cloud to expanding choice and flexibility, we’re giving organizations the tools they need to bring complex, multi-agent AI workflows into production safely.

Here’s a quick look at the major milestones, expert insights, and practical developer guides to read through and save. 

Top announcements 

  • Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud, built to help solve your business’ hardest problems: We trained Argon to work with both depth and precision, which allows it to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks which are reinforced with strong domain expertise along the way. Whether your team is running complex software builds, handling detailed financial and legal work, or deploying cybersecurity tools like CodeMender, Argon helps your teams maintain focus from start to finish. 

  • Expanding Claude availability and deployment choice on Google Cloud: We announced the general availability of an Anthropic-managed deployment option for Claude Models on Google Cloud. This gives teams more choice in how they run their models, helping them consolidate AI workloads on Google Cloud alongside our existingGoogle-managed deployment option. 

  • Google Cloud expands model choice and flexibility, bringing OpenAI models to customers: Google Cloud is now the only hyperscale cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed source LLMs, alongside more than 200 first-party, third-party, and open models on a unified enterprise AI platform. 

  • Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are now available in Google Antigravity: In keeping with Google Cloud's commitment to an open ecosystem and to give developers the right model for every job, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are now available in Google Antigravity for Google Cloud customers. Claude Opus 5.5 is built for complex work while Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a faster, lower-cost complement.

  • Introducing Gemini for government services: Today we're bringing the Gemini agent to public service with Gemini for government services in preview, part of our new suite of purpose-built industry solutions. It adds skills built around government work, connections to the systems agencies already run, and specialized partner agents, with governance running underneath it all. 

  • Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 is now available on Google Cloud: For the first time, organizations can pair Google DeepMind’s latest embodied reasoning model for robotics with the enterprise-grade security, multi-agent orchestration, and end-to-end lifecycle management of Google Cloud — making it easier to simulate, evaluate, and deploy safe, adaptive physical AI at scale.

Thought leadership (editor’s pick) 

  • A new gear: How startups are advancing robotics with Google AI: We marked a major milestone in physical AI with the launch of Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 (ER 2) on the Gemini platform and AI Studio, bringing Google DeepMind’s frontier multimodal reasoning and long-horizon task planning for robotics to Google Cloud. Read more from Darren Mowry, VP of Global Startups and Investor Ecosystem at Google, about the exciting work these startups are undertaking. 

News you can use

  • Developer’s guide to implementing MCP apps in Gemini: Enterprise assistants still respond mostly in text. However, that can break down for visual, multi-step work, where every adjustment costs another slow chat turn. This guide takes you through implementation in Gemini. 

  • Four evaluation engineering lessons learned from building agent plugins: Here are four eval lessons we learned from building the new plugin that you can apply to your own builds. 

  • Who judges the judge? Three helpful ways to audit your LLM evaluators: In this post, we explore what’s holding enterprises back from strong evals, and share an easy three-pillar method you can use to improve your quality. 

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

September

This September, we brought you new how-to guides, model updates, and security innovations to help you find-and-fix. From Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar to Mantis, there’s no shortage of new ways to apply AI to your work. 

Notably, we announced Gemini 4 Argon, our next era of frontier intelligence. Gemini 4 Argon delivers frontier performance in complex workflows across real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense. You can learn more here. 

Top announcements 

  • Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar is now generally available: Following our announcement of Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking, Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar is now generally available in Gemini Enterprise.

  • Getting started with Mantis, our open-source bug finding-and-fixing harness: Available to all as an open-source framework, Mantis is part of Google’s internal approach to find and fix vulnerabilities at machine-speed. It creates a more effective scalable, context-aware repository analysis. 

Thought leadership (editor’s pick) 

  • Racers, start your agents: Formula E brings realtime AI to the edge: Chasing records at the Goodwood Hillclimb, Formula E used Gemini Enterprise, Gemma, and a Pixel phone bolted to the dash to push the envelope of AI and edge computing.

News you can use 

Best practices guide for customizing Gemini models via Reinforcement Learning (RL): In this guide, we will walk through practical best practices for using RL fine-tuning service. We'll start with a short tour of the RL training loop, how to decide if and when to use RL, and introduce how to get the most value from this approach.

Empower your agents with the Google Cloud CLI remote MCP server: Powered by the popular gcloud and bq (BigQuery) command-line tools, this new server gives AI agents immediate, broad access to command-line operations for managing Google Cloud infrastructure and working with advanced BigQuery workflows securely and seamlessly. 

Graph Workflows in ADK: Everything you need to know: Using a refund workflow in ADK, we'll cover fan-out and fan-in, deterministic and agent routers, human-in-the-loop pauses, parallel workers, and dynamic orchestration— along with when to use a static graph or let Python decide what runs next.

August

This month, we focused on making AI highly practical for your business, including its associated costs. This meant tailoring our models for specialized industries – starting with Financial Services and Legal –  and helping you keep your budgets under control. Let’s dive in! 

Top announcements

  • FinOps for the AI era: New flexible billing and cost controls for agents: To help you get better return on AI, we announced expanded billing flexibility and new cost management tools for agent workloads across Gemini Enterprise and developer tools like Google Antigravity in Gemini Enterprise and Android Studio. 

  • Gemini Enterprise for Financial Services: We’re bringing Google’s agentic AI directly into the workflows of capital markets and corporate banking.

  • Gemini Enterprise for Legal: Gemini Enterprise for Legal provides an integrated, fully governed environment configured for rapid deployment across firms and corporate legal departments. 

  • Expanding Google Antigravity for enterprise customers: Antigravity is available now as part of eligible Gemini Enterprise app subscriptions, including out-of-the-box administrative and spend controls.

Thought leadership (editor’s pick): 

  • Tokenomics: Why smart teams spend more on AI, on purpose: Hear from Eric Lam, Head of Value, Delta, Google Cloud Consulting about how disciplined organizations are moving past reactive sticker shock over AI bills and embracing tokenomics. 

  • Meet the researcher fighting AI hallucinations at Google Cloud: Cyrus is a senior research scientist at Google. Lately, his focus has shifted to large language models, specifically a persistent issue known as hallucination, which is when an artificial intelligence model lacks the correct facts but confidently invents an answer anyway.

  • What sports cars can teach us about optimizing AI spend: More tokens doesn't always mean better AI. Read our conversation with Mike Clark, Director of Product Management for Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, on how to balance horsepower with efficiency and get the highest return out of every dollar you spend on AI.

News you can use: 

Looking for a steer on your foundation or inspiration for your next project? Take a look at some of our favorite how-to guides from August:

Each question ends with a short, runnable snippet you can copy into your own project today. Adjacent decisions that matter just as much but aren't specific to that move, your data layer and RAG architecture, CI/CD, network design, are deliberately out of frame here.

  • Your chance to start building AI agents from the absolute basics: Agent Valley is a free, 5-week live learning series designed to take you from scratch to building your very own hands-on agent systems. And instead of staring at boring terminal lines, you’ll be building and playing inside a tiny, low-poly virtual world!

July

Since launching the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform a few months ago, we’ve watched businesses move from basic experiments to serious, production-grade builds. We want to make it even easier — and more secure — for you to scale those systems.

Along with a batch of new platform updates, this month we’ve put together 13 practical demos and 20 diagnostic questions to help your engineering teams align on a strong architectural blueprint. Let’s dive in! 

Top announcements

  • What’s new in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: In this helpful recap, we announced some of our most popular capabilities are available for everyone, from Agent Runtime to Agent Identity.

  • Now in preview: Find and fix software vulnerabilities with CodeMender: As adversarial AI threats accelerate attacks on code, security teams must counter them with machine-speed defenses that can automate code remediation and fight AI with AI. You can learn more about CodeMender and review the documentation here.

  • Solve harder problems with AlphaEvolve, now available to everyone on Google Cloud: AlphaEvolve is a code optimization and discovery agent built on top of Gemini that helps solve the hardest algorithmic problems and achieve breakthroughs for your business and research. 

Thought leadership (editor’s pick): 

If automation requires delegation, then delegation requires trust. But letting an AI agent run on its own is a big leap for any business. While the productivity gains are clear, the fear of losing control is very real. This month, we sat down with our experts to discuss how leaders can navigate this shift by focusing on transparency, predictability, and setting clear boundaries for how agents handle weird data exceptions.

Here’s our picks for the month to learn more.

  • How leaders can scale AI by trading control for trust (Q&A): We sat down with Michael Gerstenhaber, VP of Product Management for Gemini Enterprise, to discuss why the future of AI is about defining safe boundaries.

  • What makes an AI agent trustworthy: Context is fast becoming one of the most valuable assets a company owns. Prajakta Damle, Senior Director, Product Management, shares what it takes to get trustworthy AI right. 

News you can use:

  • Why AI apps fail in production (And how Google solved it): Only 5% of AI prototypes make it to production, and the other 95% fall into the validation abyss. How can you move confidently into production? 

  • 13 hands-on demos to build on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: Not sure where to start with Agent Platform? Here’s 13 ways you can stir up some creativity.

June

Our main focus in June was helping your teams build, scale, and secure AI. Today, we’re sharing a fresh roundup of updates designed to help you run smarter, more secure applications while keeping everything under your control. 

We even shared a cool virtual shopping demo at Cannes to show how retailers can make product discovery more exciting. Let’s dive in! 

Top announcements

  • Introducing the Open Knowledge Format: We introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that formalizes the LLM-wiki pattern into a portable, interoperable format. This is a vendor-neutral, agent- and human-friendly standard for representing the metadata, context, and curated knowledge that modern AI systems need.

  • Collaboration with Apple on its expanded Private Cloud Compute (PCC) systems: Our collaboration with Apple is built on a foundation of deep commitment to privacy that leverages Google Cloud's security and privacy technologies. At the heart of this collaboration is our Confidential Computing portfolio and our Titanium security architecture.

  • Claude Fable 5: Available on Google Cloud: Claude Fable 5, Anthropic’s latest frontier model, is now generally available on Google Cloud. This launch is the latest proof point of our ongoing commitment to bring the industry's latest models straight to our Agent Platform. 

  • Cloud Atelier: How Gemini Enterprise is helping restyle the retail playbook: This year at Cannes, we showcased Cloud Atelier — a destination-based, virtual shopping experience that highlights how retail brands can turn this classic dilemma into an exciting moment of product discovery. 

Thought leadership (editor’s pick): 

  • How Google Cloud Security uses AI internally: To counter machine-speed, AI-driven threats, we’ve worked hard to transition Google Cloud’s security posture to an autonomous, proactive model. By embedding specialized AI agents directly into our software development lifecycle (SDLC), we’ve created automated guardrails that protect code at a scale and speed unreachable by human teams — and we’re taking steps to make those same guardrails widely available.

  • The 4 lessons that guided AI Threat Defense: We introduced Chris Betz as the new CISO of Google Cloud. For his first Cloud CISO Perspectives, Chris shares four key lessons we learned about using AI to the defender’s advantage while building AI Threat Defense.

News you can use: 

  • 5 lessons from red teaming AI applications: To help you build AI securely, Mandiant has developed a proactive, risk-based approach centered on the Good AI Assessment (GAIA) Top 10, outlined in our new report, Secure Development of Generative AI Applications: A Proactive Approach. 

  • How to unlock true ROI in software development – a deep dive into the latest DORA research: To help you evaluate the costs and business benefits of AI, we recently shared the DORA: ROI of AI-assisted software development report. This research offers a practical approach to help your team work through early adoption challenges, align engineering plans, and drive business growth.

  • Agent Factory Recap: 100X engineering with AI agents in Google Antigravity 2.0: In this episode of the Agent Factory, Shir Meir Lador, Head of AI Engineering, Google Cloud Developer Relations, sat down with Rody Davis, one of Google’s top agentic engineers. They dive into the massive shift from traditional IDEs to agent-first platforms, the reality of code reviews in an AI-driven world, and how to use "skills" to perform at a 100X level.

April

We hosted Google Cloud Next in Las Vegas on April 22, announcing incredible innovations from Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to our eight-generation TPUs. We also expanded the Gemini Enterprise app in collaborative ways – now, with new features like Projects, you can work side-by-side with your agents and colleagues. 

If you missed the livestream, take a look at our Day 1 recap. It’s been incredible to see how customers have been applying AI in thousands of ways — so far, we’ve counted more than 1,300 examples. 

Top announcements

1. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: Our new, comprehensive platform to build, scale, govern, and optimize agents. Moving forward, all Vertex AI services and roadmap evolutions will be delivered exclusively through the Agent Platform, rather than as a standalone service, to power the next generation of agent development.

The platform is designed around four core pillars — build, scale, govern, and optimize — that allow teams to collaborate seamlessly. Learn more about Agent Platform here.

2. Gemini Enterprise app has all the key components to let teams discover, create, share, and run AI agents in a single environment. At Next ‘26, we introduced several new capabilities in the Gemini Enterprise app:

  • Agent Designer uses the same no-code agent designer experience of Agent Platform and lets employees build sophisticated schedule- and trigger-based agents using any enterprise connector. It gives you a virtual flowchart of your agent, allowing you to inspect, test, and approve workflows, ensuring total transparency for executing critical business processes.  

  • Long-running agents are designed to execute complex business processes. They can work autonomously in secure cloud sandboxes, giving agents the ability to orchestrate business logic, write code to build custom tools, and complete multi-step work like reconciliation activities or sales prospect sequencing — without needing constant prompting. 

  • Inbox in Gemini Enterprise provides a central location to monitor, guide, and help manage all of your agent activity, including your long-running agents. Notifications are intuitively categorized into actionable groups like "Needs your input," "Errors," and "Completed.” 

  • Projects create a dedicated space where the agent’s memory is confined to the files and conversations your team adds. By connecting it to data sources including Google Drive, NotebookLM, and Google Group Chats, the agent becomes an expert on a specific topic and can provide team members daily briefings or status updates without digging through months of documents.

  • Skills create simple shortcuts using an “@” mention for repetitive tasks such as applying brand guidelines, formatting a report, and accessing specific data.

  • Canvas gives our customers an interactive editor directly within Gemini Enterprise. It allows teams to easily create and edit Docs and Slides, and even export to Microsoft 365 files, within the same experience. 

  • Agent Gallery provides access to third-party agents from partners like Adobe, Atlassian, Lovable, and ServiceNow, and is adding more third-party connectors for Asana, Mailchimp, Workday, and more. These integrations enable your agents to retrieve data and execute tasks with your systems-of-record. 

3. AI Hypercomputer: Designed specifically for demanding AI workloads, our AI Hypercomputer is an advanced, purpose-built architecture that unites performance-optimized hardware for compute, storage, networking, open software and machine learning frameworks — as well as flexible consumption models — into a single, integrated system. We are announcing innovations at every layer of the AI Hypercomputer:

  • TPU 8t, optimized for training, uses breakthrough Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) technology to scale up to 9,600 TPUs and 2 PB of shared, high-bandwidth memory in a single superpod. It achieves 3x the processing power of Ironwood and delivers up to 2x more performance/Watt. 
  • TPU 8i, optimized for inference, uses our new Boardfly topology to directly connect 1,152 TPUs in a single pod. It features 3x more on-chip SRAM compared to previous versions to host larger KV caches entirely on-silicon and integrates a specialized Collectives Acceleration Engine. Taken together, TPU 8i delivers 80% better performance per dollar for inference than the prior generation, enabling millions of concurrent agents to run cost-effectively.

4. The Agentic Data Cloud: A new data architecture built for the speed and scale of agentic AI. The Agentic Data Cloud delivers an AI-native architecture, allowing agents to perceive, reason, and act on your behalf in real-time, including: 

  • Cross-Cloud Lakehouse, standardized on Apache Iceberg, is our Lakehouse that enables you to leave your data in AWS or Azure (coming later this year) while querying it instantly — without the friction of vendor lock-in or the cost of data movement

  • Knowledge Catalog constructs a unified, dynamic context graph of your entire business enabling you to ground agents in all of your business data and semantics. With Smart Storage and the Object Context API, files in Google Cloud Storage are instantly tagged and enriched with metadata before an agent touches them. Then our Knowledge Engine uses Gemini to autonomously tag, define logic and instantly map complex relationships across your entire enterprise, providing the semantic definition your agents have been missing. 

5. Protecting the agentic enterprise: Security built for the AI era. Our full-stack AI approach, from the chips to the models, gives you a competitive advantage with better integration and velocity to help protect customers. Not only can Google action insights from the world’s largest threat observatory and Mandiant frontline experts, but we also bring cutting-edge insights and breakthroughs from Google DeepMind, to help make your platforms more secure.

  • Agentic defense: Three new agents in Google Security Operations can help hunt threats, engineer detections, and provide context on third parties. You can build your own security agents with remote Google Cloud model context protocol (MCP) server support for Google Security Operations, now generally available. You can also access the MCP server client directly from the Google Security Operations chat interface, available in preview.
  • Protecting AI and cloud apps across any infrastructure with Wiz: Newly expanded AI coverage helps build secure agents across clouds and AI studios. New AI-Bill of Materials in development tools can help secure AI-generated code and mitigate the risk of shadow AI. Learn more.
  • Securing agents and the agentic web: Model Armor can integrate with Agent Gateway, and new Agent Identities provide more layers of defense against shadow AI. Google Cloud Fraud Defense, the next evolution of reCAPTCHA, offers agent-specific capabilities that can help secure the agentic web as well as the entire user and customer journey.   
  • Trusted Cloud: We’re simplifying permissions with modern IAM, and advancing Google Cloud security with new capabilities in Security Command Center plus new innovations in data and network security.
  • New partner-supported workflows for Google Security Operations: This new robust cohort of partner integrations includes partners developing their own agentic security operations centers (SOCs).

You can catch up on all our security announcements from Next ‘26 here.

We'll share how to get strong results from the model, whether you are building accessible gaming soundtracks, banking systems, or audiobooks. Learn more about the model here.

March

March was a busy month for our AI teams. We launched Gemini Embedding 2, rolled out a highly cost-effective Veo 3.1 Lite model, and officially welcomed the Wiz team to Google Cloud to help redefine security in the AI era. 

Alongside these launches, we created comprehensive guides to help you get the most out of these models, from prompting formulas for Nano Banana 2, to practical advice for optimizing your TPU training. Here’s a quick look at the latest news and resources to help your team build what’s next.

Top hits: 

  • Gemini Embedding 2: Our first natively multimodal embedding model: Gemini Embedding 2 is our first natively multimodal embedding model that maps text, images, video, audio and documents into a single embedding space, enabling multimodal retrieval and classification across different types of media — and it’s available now in public preview.
  • Build with Veo 3.1 Lite, our most cost-effective video generation model: This model empowers developers to build high-volume video applications, at less than 50% of the cost of Veo 3.1 Fast, but with the same speed. This rounds out the Veo 3.1 model family, giving developers flexibility based on needs. For Cloud customers, it’s now available on Vertex AI. 

Here’s a fun bonus: Check out our ultimate prompting guide for Veo 3.1 to get started.

  • Welcoming Wiz to Google Cloud: Redefining security for the AI era: Google has completed its acquisition of Wiz, a leading cloud and AI security platform. The Wiz team will join Google Cloud, and we will retain the Wiz brand. With the addition of Wiz, we will provide customers with a comprehensive platform to secure their cloud and hybrid environments, as well as accelerate threat prevention, detection, and response.
  • Gemini 3.1 Flash Live: Making audio AI more natural and reliable: We’ve improved 3.1 Flash Live’s overall quality, making it more reliable for developers and enterprises to build voice-first agents that can complete complex tasks at scale. On ComplexFuncBench Audio, a benchmark that captures multi-step function calling with various constraints, it leads with a score of 90.8% compared to our previous model.

We’re also opening up new training programs and step-by-step guides to help you tackle the hardest parts of the AI lifecycle, from capacity planning to mounting defenses against AI-powered attacks.

Here’s a rundown of our latest news, tools, and resources to help you build what’s next.

Top hits

  • Introducing Gemini 3.1 Pro on Google Cloud: Gemini 3.1 Pro is a clear step forward in reasoning, designed to solve tougher problems, giving you the reasoning depth your business needs. Gemini 3.1 Pro is available starting today in preview in Vertex AI and Gemini Enterprise. Developers can access the model in preview via the Gemini API in Google AI Studio, Android Studio, Google Antigravity, and Gemini CLI.

content_excerpt: Lyngvi is a hardened, agent-agnostic sandbox for running autonomous coding agents against your own repositories. You drive it from a desktop app — the conversation, the diff and the delivery in one window — or from the command line, which is the same product without the window. The agent gets a working copy, a toolchain and a controlled way out. It never gets your credentials, your git history or a route to the internet. Everything the app does is also a command. The CLI ships inside the app and in a package of its own, and both call the same core: Named after the island in Norse mythology where the wolf Fenrir was bound: a place where great power is kept within defined boundaries. Making a sandbox, talking to the agent, reading the diff and delivering what you approve are all in the app, and none of it needs the terminal. Every screen below is the real JavaFX app, run against a sandbox with one repository, three conversations and a change waiting to be reviewed. No mock-ups, no retouching. Every reply shows what the agent read, searched, ran and edited — with +/− counts on each edit — and what the turn cost in tokens and dollars. The strip above the composer says what is waiting for delivery, and that one file is held back. Everything else in Lyngvi is shell around these four. They are the reason an agent can run unattended in a repository you care about. The session container sits on an internal network with no default route. Every outbound connection goes through a Squid proxy with an allowlist, and an explicit blocklist of known exfiltration endpoints is evaluated first. The agent works in a copy with a fresh .git — no hooks, no config, no remotes, no credential helper. The whole git attack surface is removed structurally, not by policy. Internal systems are reached through a read-only, allowlisted API that holds the token. The agent only ever sees a hostname. A plugin cannot read the secret: the runtime injects it into a locked upstream object. Changes come back as a patch, classified on the host file by file, reviewed by you, and committed to a working branch. Never to main, never silently. All logic lives in a Java core that both the CLI and the JavaFX GUI call in-process. The core is the only thing that talks to git and Podman. title: AI evals for agents: what they are and how to write them
story_key: story|title:ai evals for agents what they are and how to write them
content_excerpt: AI evals are tests that grade what a model or agent did. How agent evals differ from LLM evals, the three grader types, and how to write one in 7 steps. An AI eval is a test for an AI system: you give it an input, let it run, and grade what it did with code, with another model, or with a person. LLM evals grade a single response. Evals for AI agents grade a whole run: the tools the agent called, the arguments it passed, the state it left behind and the reply it ended with. That difference decides how you write them, because an agent can reply "your refund is on its way" without ever calling the refund tool, and an eval that reads only the reply will mark that run as a pass. This guide defines the parts of an eval, explains how agent evals differ from LLM evals, covers the three kinds of grader, and then walks through writing an eval for an agent in seven steps, with a worked example you can adapt. Anthropic's guide to agent evals ( Demystifying evals for AI agents ↗ , January 2026) uses a vocabulary most eval tools now share. It is worth adopting, because "the eval failed" can mean any of these: A task can have several graders, and usually should. One that checks the refund exists, one that checks policy was looked up first, and one that checks the reply explains the timeline will each fail for a different reason, and you want to know which. The terms overlap and are often used interchangeably, but they grade different things. The practical consequence: an agent's worst regressions read as correct. A model that stops calling notify_security_team , or reports an address change it never made, still writes fluent, on-topic prose. Every eval that scores the text alone passes it. What actually breaks when you switch LLMs goes through the full change surface. Every eval grader is one of three kinds, and a good suite uses all three for different jobs. The order matters. Use code for everything code can check, a model for the quality of prose that is left, and people to write the criteria, label a calibration sample and read the failures. title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.

content_excerpt: For the past two years, building capable Agents meant designing tools, figuring out which actions help the model complete a task, deciding how granular each tool schema needs to be, or iterating on system instruction templates. This is changing. Agents are moving in the opposite direction by collapsing their entire tool catalog into one tool : exec . This is called Code Mode (or Programmatic Tool Calling). Instead of forcing the model to trigger tools one at a time across turns, the harness gives the model a single exec(code) tool. The model writes a short TypeScript or Python script that chains, combines, and awaits actions inside an isolated sandbox. To understand why agents are converging on a single exec tool, we should look at how tool calling evolved. Initially, we only gave agents a handful of tools because they couldn't reliably choose or filter across a large catalog. As models improved, we connected dozens of tools or MCP servers, but ran into context window limits. We solved that with tool search and progressive disclosure , letting agents look up tools on demand. Even with dynamic tool loading, we still had dozens of individual tools, and were still stuck with the limitation of standard tool calling: one action per turn. In standard tool calling, the model generates a structured object (typically JSON) that defines a single action (or at best a flat batch of independent calls, like reading three files), waits for the raw output to come back, adds it into the prompt history, reasons again, and decides what to do next. From my own experience, we made a big jump recently in how reliably models can combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass: Several shifts came together to enable this. Frontier models are trained heavily on code, and providers have started post-training models for Code Mode. At the same time, MCP servers now increasingly ship outputSchema alongside inputSchema , giving the model upfront knowledge of return types so it can chain Tool A into Tool B inside the same script before seeing runtime output. Code Mode collapses the tool catalog into a single tool on the model surface: exec(code) . Instead of passing 80 separate JSON Schema tool objects to the model API, the agent compiles those schemas into compact type declarations ( declare namespace tools { ... } ). summary: Arca's head of AI discusses persistent memory, the benefits of a custom harness, and agentic workflows that span days.

Arca's head of AI discusses persistent memory, the benefits of a custom harness, and agentic workflows that span days. At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh , the lead AI Engineer at Arca , an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that human advisors are making the final decisions. The goal is for AI to guide the process; or as Singh nicely put it, “agents prompt people more than people prompt agents.” Arca recently raised $48.5 Million in a round led by General Catalyst, with participation from Index Ventures and Venrock. One of the features of using AI in financial services, explained Singh, is that it’s typically long-horizon work — although not long-running. In his AIE presentation, Singh noted that agent tasks at Arca can take up to ten days. “It's very stop-start, there's many actors in between, many decision points, many handoffs,” he said. “So we have this persistence for every client ,” Singh said in our podcast discussion. “What has happened so far? What are we tracking for next? What needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days [and] what are we tracking for the long term? Which individual is responsible for which action? All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.” Arca uses models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with Claude its primary model provider. The company has built its own harness , which automatically selects the best model to use for a particular task, based on the company’s internal benchmarks. Owning the harness, rather than using a managed agent harness, also means that Arca has the flexibility to change model providers if it needs to. Safety is obviously key for financial services. Singh noted that although agents do much of the work, an agent’s role is limited to analysis and proposing solutions. Trading and any other money movement is handled by a human advisor. “All of our safety restrictions are fully deterministic,” he said. “And they take the decision making off the agent's hands.”

title: Text as an Index for Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Knowledge Tracing
summary: Knowledge tracing (KT) predicts a student's next response from their history. New platforms often have question texts but no response logs for training, motivating zero-shot cross-domain KT. Existing transfer and cold-start methods use question semantics, but cross-platform semantic discrepancies limit transferability. We propose TIZSKT, which separates behavioral sequence modeling from domain-local historical evidence construction and uses text as an index rather than a directly transferable predictive representation. The Mastery-Dynamics Encoder learns correctness dynamics without question identifiers or text embeddings. Domain-Local Question Addressing builds fixed question addresses using a frozen text encoder and an unsupervised per-domain projection. The Text-Addressing Kernel uses these addresses to aggregate the current student's previous outcomes into a question-specific historical correctness summary. Cross-Segment Continuation retains access to earlier responses without extending the behavioral encoder's input sequence. Evidence-Volume Read-Out preserves the total kernel mass discarded by normalization and combines its log-compressed value with the behavioral state and historical correctness summary to predict the next response. All trainable parameters are learned from source domains; target inference uses public question texts and the current student's observed history without target-domain training. Leave-one-domain-out experiments on three public datasets show that TIZSKT achieves the highest mean AUC and accuracy among evaluated baselines on all target domains. Ablations confirm the contributions of text addressing and cross-segment continuation.

title: RangeSWA: Training-Free Length Extrapolation for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
summary: Continuous diffusion language models show promising potential in text generation tasks, but are prone to problems such as text repetition, semantic drift, and generation quality degradation when the generation length exceeds the training length. To address these challenges, we propose RangeSWA, a training-free length extrapolation method. The method combines local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to preserve local details and support long-range context access. In addition, generation degradation caused by length extrapolation is mitigated through positional remapping, conditioning attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling. We conducted experiments on multiple continuous diffusion language models, and the results show that RangeSWA can effectively reduce generative perplexity and text repetition rates in long-text generation.

title: Evaluating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks
summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.

title: RAMA: Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent Routing with Episodic Memory for LEO Satellite Networks
summary: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks present a challenging routing environment due to rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) routing methods typically rely on current observations and information encoded in network weights, limiting their ability to exploit successful past experiences. We propose RAMA, a retrieval-augmented multi-agent DRL framework with Approximate Information State (AIS), in which each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, neighboring state information, and retrieved entries from a per-satellite episodic memory. Retrieved experiences are integrated through a Transformer-based decision network trained with AIS-based auxiliary objectives. With weights frozen in a 140-satellite Kepler constellation, RAMA reduces mean end-to-end latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% relative to the state-of-theart double deep Q-network (DDQN) routing method, mainly by avoiding long detours. Updated online, RAMA remains stable while DDQN degrades. On the 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1, the reduction in mean latency grows to 93.2%, and updating RAMA online lowers its mean latency by a further 25.5%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented memory for scalable decentralized routing in LEO satellite networks.

title: Optimizing Stochastic Policy Geometry for Few-Step Flow Reinforcement Learning
summary: Few-step flow models generate samples through a handful of large denoising transitions. Applying GRPO to such models requires introducing stochasticity into the denoising transitions, and when a single transition spans a wide range of noise levels, the choice of the resulting stochastic policy becomes a major factor in optimization. Recent constructions constrain the policy to preserve the target flow coefficients, but this constraint admits a family of policies and offers no criterion for choosing among them. We introduce Geo-FSRL (Geometry-Optimized Few-Step Reinforcement Learning), built on a selection principle: at a fixed conditioning state and timestep pair, choose the admissible policy that minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by any given nonzero velocity-output update. Within a coefficient-preserving family of isotropic Gaussian transitions, this criterion reduces to minimizing a single scalar geometry factor that determines the conditional KL for every velocity-output update. The same factor governs velocity-space Fisher information and conditional transition log-likelihood-ratio variance. We derive the unique closed-form optimizer within this family, shared across all nonzero update magnitudes and directions, with transition coefficients determined by both the source and target noise levels. Because the minimized geometry factor still varies across timesteps, we further adopt gradient-scale matching from prior work and derive closed-form policy-gradient and KL weights that normalize explicit score scales and reference-KL curvature. Geo-FSRL trains on the original few-step schedule and retains the deterministic solver at inference. Our method achieves higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image generation and video generation models under the 4-step setting. summary: Genie 4: our new world model unlocking unprecedented realism in real-time simulation.
story_key: story|title:genie 4 a new generation of world simulation
content_excerpt: Today, we are announcing Genie 4, our new world model, which unlocks unprecedented realism and improves real-time interactive simulation. Genie 4 is natively multimodal, enabling audio-like music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue to be simultaneously generated with the world. The Genie 4 model incorporates and builds on capabilities from the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models provide the complex reasoning needed to help maintain a simulation’s coherence and continuity. With this foundation, you can set an event in motion, and Genie 4 simulates what happens next: how the world responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak. Understanding and simulating the world is a crucial aspect of building AGI. Genie 4 advances our ability to create safe, infinitely variable simulations that can help with everything from developing training environments for robots and agents to unlocking the creation of new interactive experiences. We have started rolling Genie 4 out as a research preview for trusted testers — gathering feedback before we release it to consumers and developers, starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie here . Genie 4 delivers enhanced photorealism, fluid movement, and native audio. All accompanying sounds featured above are produced directly by Genie 4. The following are recordings of real-time interactions from Genie 4, where users use standard keyboard controls for navigation and camera control, and text prompts to steer the scene as it evolves. With Genie 4, you can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time — like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object — and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene. Between your inputs, Gemini also monitors and steers the scene to keep the world progressing cohesively. Prompt: Use the reference image as the exact first frame and visual basis for the scene. What's changed

  • Added oidc.user_id_claim to the Claude apps gateway, to identify people by an id_token claim other than sub, such as Microsoft Entra ID's oid
  • Added click to send: in fullscreen, clicking the "to send now" hint under a queued message sends it right away, as its key does
  • Fixed managed settings and organization policy not being fetched for the rest of the session after signing in from the VS Code extension
  • Fixed Claude overwriting a very large CLAUDE.md, rules file or @-included file in a subdirectory after seeing only its start; Write now asks Claude to read it all or edit in place
  • Fixed per-directory and paths: skills not being found after a Bash cd deeper into a git repository
  • Fixed a rare case where the first reply after resuming a session in the terminal could be missing the next time the session was resumed
  • Fixed a command with an invalid name stopping all commands from loading, which could leave claude -p with no output
  • Fixed the Read tool sometimes failing on PDF pages with "pdftoppm failed: Could not write image" when the clean-up of old session files ran at the same time
  • Fixed the spinner, OpenTelemetry effort values and transcripts naming a newly picked effort level during a task before the model applied it; they now show the level in force
  • Fixed the /model and /effort cache warning saying the re-read waits for your next message; a change made while Claude is working can trigger it sooner
  • Fixed some sessions showing as waiting on you when the last message only mentioned items waiting on you mid-sentence
  • Fixed agent view restoring input text on the next launch after it was cleared with Ctrl+C just before exiting
  • Fixed agent view reopening in shell mode after exiting with Ctrl+D from an empty ! input
  • Fixed vim mode d, c and y with a gj or gk count larger than the lines left deleting or copying text; like Vim, they now only move the cursor
  • Fixed /verify showing a long description meant for Claude in /help and the / command menu instead of a short one
  • Improved the prompt's effort indicator: a change made mid-task now says it may wait for your next message, and the note clears when it no longer applies

  • Changed Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle to use the shorter system prompt for model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names and inference profile ARNs, even when they front Sonnet or Haiku; set CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 to keep the full prompt

  • [VSCode] Changed usage limit resets to show a clock time ("Resets at 3:10 PM") and to say "5-hour limit"
